  "interactive_layout": "# The Wall With No Room to Spare

*An interactive tour of the Umans–Wang $(\alpha,\beta)$-divisor conjecture: what it asks, where its counting limit really lies, and why the target sits exactly on that limit.*

## 1. The game

You are given the numbers $1,2,\dots,n$. You **catch** a number $i$ by producing a multiple of $i$. The catch: your multiples must be **differences** $s-t$ of two small sets $S$ and $T$.

> **Definition (the $n$-divisor property).** $(S,T)$ has the $n$-divisor property if every $1\le i\le n$ divides some positive difference $s-t$ with $s\in S$, $t\in T$.

Try it. The preset $S=\{17,21\}$, $T=\{1,3\}$ catches everything up to $10$. Exhaustive search shows that no pair of two-element sets with smaller entries does. Then try the random preset and watch the red cells pile up.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Umans and Wang ([arXiv:2511.10851](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10851)) ask how cheap such a certificate can be:

> **Conjecture ($(\alpha,\beta)$-divisor).** For infinitely many $n$ there are $S,T\subseteq\mathbb Z^+$ with the $n$-divisor property, all elements at most $e^{n^\alpha}$, and $|S|,|T|\le n^\beta$.

The point that matters for their application is $\alpha=\beta=\tfrac13$.

## 2. The counting wall, in four lines

The idea is that **everything you catch must divide the product of your differences.**

1. Each $i\le n$ divides some difference, so $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$ divides the product $P$ of all positive differences.
2. There are at most $|S||T|$ differences, each below $M=\max S$, so $P\le M^{|S||T|}$.
3. $\binom{2m}{m}$ divides $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,2m)$ and $\binom{2m}{m}\ge 4^m/(2m+1)$.
4. Hence $4^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\le (n+1)M^{|S||T|}$.

<details><summary><b>Why every prime power in $\binom{2m}{m}$ is at most $2m$</b></summary>

By [Legendre's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_formula), the exponent of $p$ in $\binom{2m}{m}$ is $\sum_{j\ge1}\big(\lfloor 2m/p^j\rfloor-2\lfloor m/p^j\rfloor\big)$. Each term is $0$ or $1$, and it vanishes once $p^j>2m$. So $p^e\le 2m$, and $p^e$ is one of the numbers whose lcm is $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,2m)$. The bound $\binom{2m}{m}\ge4^m/(2m+1)$ holds because $\binom{2m}{m}$ is the largest of the $2m+1$ terms summing to $4^m$.
</details>

With $M=e^{n^\alpha}$ and $|S|,|T|\le n^\beta$, take logarithms:
$$(n-1)\log 2\;\le\;\log(n+1)+n^{\alpha+2\beta}.$$
The left side is linear in $n$. If $\alpha+2\beta<1$, the right side is eventually smaller.

{{visualization:1}}

> **Theorem (corrected counting constraint).** If the conjecture's sets exist for infinitely many $n$, then $\alpha\ge 1-2\beta$.

<details><summary><b>The full proof of the asymptotic step</b></summary>

Suppose $\gamma=\alpha+2\beta<1$. The functions $\log(x+1)$, $x^\gamma$ and $\log2$ are each $o(x)$, so for all large $x$ their sum is less than $x\log 2$. In particular $\log(n+1)+n^\gamma<(n-1)\log2$ for all large integers $n$. The hypothesis supplies arbitrarily large $n$ that admit a cover. For such an $n$ the logarithmic wall gives the opposite inequality, which is a contradiction.
</details>

**The correction.** The boundary is the line $\alpha+2\beta=1$. It is **not** "$\alpha+\beta\le1$". The factor $2$ is there because two sets of size $n^\beta$ produce $n^{2\beta}$ differences.

## 3. Zero slack

Put $\beta=\tfrac13$. Then $1-2\beta=\tfrac13=\alpha$, so the target lies **exactly on the wall**. Explore the exponent square below and drop the point a hair below the red line.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

{{visualization:0}}

This explains why the exponent $\tfrac16$ in the application is a floor. It is where the counting wall sits.

## 4. The trivial line, and why it is almost optimal

Cut $[n]$ into blocks of length $b$, let $S=\{1+\prod(\text{block})\}$ and $T=\{1\}$.

> **Theorem (block cover).** $(S,T)$ has the $n$-divisor property, $|S|\le\lceil n/b\rceil$, and $\max S\le 1+n^b$. With $b=n^{1-\beta}$ this gives $\alpha=1-\beta+o(1)$.

{{algorithm:1}}

Here $|S||T|\log M\approx\frac nb\cdot b\log n=n\log n$, which is within a factor $\log n$ of the wall. So **the wall is essentially tight for unbalanced covers.** The conjecture needs *balanced* sets, whose $|S||T|$ differences carry only $|S|+|T|-1$ degrees of freedom, because $(s_1-t_1)-(s_1-t_2)=(s_2-t_1)-(s_2-t_2)$. The open problem is a **balancing** problem.

## 5. Is the wall ever met exactly?

> **Theorem (singleton optimum).** For $|S|=|T|=1$ and $t\ge1$, the least possible $s$ is exactly $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)+1$.

Load the "|S|=|T|=1 optimum" preset in the playground: the budget bar is full. For two-element sets, exhaustive search stays within a factor $3$ of the wall $\operatorname{lcm}(1,\dots,n)^{1/4}$ for $n\le10$.

{{visualization:2}}

{{algorithm:3}}

{{algorithm:0}}

## 6. A tempting shortcut: progressions that hit every prime

Umans and Wang's Lemma 6.2 builds an arithmetic progression $b+c,\dots,b+\ell c$ whose terms are divisible by the blocks $U_i$ of a factorization of the primorial $U=\prod_{p\le n}p$.

> **Theorem (CRT progression).** For pairwise coprime $U_0,\dots,U_{\ell-1}$ and any step $c$, some $b$ satisfies $U_i\mid b+(i+1)c$ for all $i$.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details><summary><b>Why a 2-term progression hitting every prime proves nothing</b></summary>

The statement holds with $\ell=1$: the primorial itself is a one-term progression divisible by every prime. For $n=10$, the progression $20,21$ hits $2,5$ and $3,7$, but so does $210$ alone. The divisor property needs every $i\le n$, prime powers included, to divide a difference of two small sets. All the difficulty lies in the size of $b$ and $c$. The paper's Lemma 6.3 shows that generic inputs force either $\ell'\ge M^{\Omega(1)}$ terms or terms of size $M^{\log\log M}$, so only structured factorizations can work.
</details>

## 7. Run the numbers yourself

The script below reproduces every number on this page: the walls on explicit covers, the singleton and two-by-two optima, the exponent table, the CRT progressions, and a random $(\tfrac13,\tfrac13)$ experiment. In that experiment random sets cover at best about $27$–$39\%$ of $[n]$, and never all of it.

{{demo:0}}

## 8. What remains open

*For infinitely many $n$, construct structured sets $S,T$ with $|S|,|T|\le n^{1/3}$ and elements at most $e^{n^{1/3}}$ whose differences catch every $i\le n$.* The counting wall says nothing smaller is possible. The trivial cover shows that counting is tight when the sets are lopsided. Whether balance can be achieved is the whole question. See the Future Directions tab for concrete attacks: two-dimensional progression grids, balanced–unbalanced transfer, and an additive-rank wall.

namespace UMWWall

open Finset Real Filter

/-- The `n`-divisor property for the difference set `S − T`: every `1 ≤ i ≤ n` divides some
nonzero difference.  Since `i ∣ s − t ↔ i ∣ t − s`, we orient differences positively,
`t < s`, and work in `ℕ`. -/
def DivisorProperty (n : ℕ) (S T : Finset ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i, 1 ≤ i → i ≤ n → ∃ s ∈ S, ∃ t ∈ T, t < s ∧ i ∣ s - t

/-- `lcm(1, …, n)`. -/
def lcmUpTo (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (Icc 1 n).lcm id

/-- Product of all positive differences `s − t`, `s ∈ S`, `t ∈ T`, `t < s`. -/
def diffProd (S T : Finset ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ∏ p ∈ (S ×ˢ T).filter (fun p => p.2 < p.1), (p.1 - p.2)

lemma diffProd_pos (S T : Finset ℕ) : 0 < diffProd S T := by
  unfold diffProd
  refine Finset.prod_pos ?_
  intro p hp
  have := (Finset.mem_filter.mp hp).2
  omega

/-- Every forced divisor divides the product of differences, hence so does their lcm. -/
theorem lcm_dvd_diffProd {n : ℕ} {S T : Finset ℕ} (h : DivisorProperty n S T) :
    lcmUpTo n ∣ diffProd S T := by
  unfold lcmUpTo
  refine Finset.lcm_dvd ?_
  intro i hi
  obtain ⟨hi1, hin⟩ := Finset.mem_Icc.mp hi
  obtain ⟨s, hs, t, ht, hts, hdvd⟩ := h i hi1 hin
  have hmem : (s, t) ∈ (S ×ˢ T).filter (fun p => p.2 < p.1) :=
    Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨Finset.mem_product.mpr ⟨hs, ht⟩, hts⟩
  exact hdvd.trans (Finset.dvd_prod_of_mem (fun p : ℕ × ℕ => p.1 - p.2) hmem)

theorem diffProd_le {S T : Finset ℕ} {M : ℕ} (hM : 1 ≤ M) (hS : ∀ s ∈ S, s ≤ M) :
    diffProd S T ≤ M ^ (S.card * T.card) := by
  unfold diffProd
  calc ∏ p ∈ (S ×ˢ T).filter (fun p => p.2 < p.1), (p.1 - p.2)
      ≤ M ^ ((S ×ˢ T).filter (fun p => p.2 < p.1)).card := by
        refine Finset.prod_le_pow_card _ _ _ ?_
        intro p hp
        have := hS p.1 (Finset.mem_product.mp (Finset.mem_filter.mp hp).1).1
        omega
    _ ≤ M ^ (S ×ˢ T).card := Nat.pow_le_pow_right hM (Finset.card_filter_le _ _)
    _ = M ^ (S.card * T.card) := by rw [Finset.card_product]

  unfold lcmUpTo
  intro h
  rw [Finset.lcm_eq_zero_iff] at h
  obtain ⟨i, hi, h0⟩ := h
  simp only [id] at h0
  have := (Finset.mem_Icc.mp hi).1
  omega

  unfold lcmUpTo
  refine Finset.lcm_dvd ?_
  intro i hi
  obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := Finset.mem_Icc.mp hi
  exact Finset.dvd_lcm (Finset.mem_Icc.mpr ⟨h1, h2.trans h⟩)

theorem centralBinom_dvd_lcm (m : ℕ) : (2 * m).choose m ∣ lcmUpTo (2 * m) := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos m with rfl | hm
  · simp
  have hpos : 0 < 2 * m := by omega
  have hc0 : (2 * m).choose m ≠ 0 := (Nat.choose_pos (by omega)).ne'

    ∏ i ∈ block n b j, i ≤ n ^ b := by

`U₀, …, U_{ℓ-1}` and any step `c`, there is a start `b` with `U_i ∣ b + (i+1)·c` for all

    (hcop : (↑(range ℓ) : Set ℕ).Pairwise (Function.onFun Nat.Coprime U)) (c : ℕ) :

  have hUi : 0 < U i := Nat.pos_of_ne_zero (hU i hmem)
  have hr : (i + 1) * c % U i < U i := Nat.mod_lt _ hUi
  have h1 : k + (i + 1) * c ≡ (U i - (i + 1) * c % U i) + (i + 1) * c % U i [MOD U i] :=
    Nat.ModEq.add (hk i hmem) (Nat.mod_modEq _ _).symm
  rw [Nat.sub_add_cancel hr.le] at h1
  exact (Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd).mp (h1.trans (Nat.modEq_zero_iff_dvd.mpr dvd_rfl))

cheap; the entire content of Umans–Wang's use of Lemma 6.2 is the *size* of `b, c`, which
this existence statement does not control (cf. Lemma 6.3). -/

    ∃ b : ℕ, ∀ p, p.Prime → p ≤ n → ∃ i < ℓ, p ∣ b + (i + 1) * c := by
  obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := crt_progression ℓ U hU hcop c

    obtain ⟨i, hi, hpi⟩ := hcover p hp hpn

        b = round(n ** (2 / 3))
